## Biography

I am a Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Economics at the University of California, Davis. **I will be on the 2026-2027 academic job market.**

My research lies at the intersection of international macroeconomics, international finance, and political economics. I study how geopolitical risk, dollar-based financial infrastructure, and firm-level financing frictions shape currency choice in global trade and the transmission of shocks across countries.

My job market paper examines how U.S. financial sanctions against Chinese entities affect dollar dominance in trade invoicing. Combining cross-country invoicing data, measures of working-capital dependence, and a quantitative model of exporters' currency choice, I investigate how risks to dollar financing can encourage a shift toward renminbi invoicing along trade links to China. I also study retailers' and households' responses to beverage taxes and health risks.

## Job Market Paper

<div class="jmp-title">Financial Sanctions and Dollar Dominance in Trade Invoicing</div>

<div class="jmp-status">Draft available upon request.</div>

<div class="jmp-takeaway">The reliability of working-capital finance helps explain how sanctions can reshape currency choice along trade links to China.</div>

<details class="abstract-toggle">
<summary>Abstract</summary>

::: {.abstract-box}
Does the use of financial sanctions weaken dollar dominance in trade invoicing? Using a panel of FX-neutral import invoicing shares for 88 countries over 2012–2023, I examine how responses to U.S. sanctions against Chinese entities vary with baseline import exposure to China. For a one-standard-deviation increase in log sanctions intensity, a 10 percentage point (pp) higher China import share is associated with a contemporaneous Chinese renminbi (RMB) response that is 0.19 pp higher and a U.S. dollar (USD) response that is 0.84 pp lower. The RMB exposure gradient is flatter among destinations whose imports from China have low working-capital intensity. I develop a model in which exporters balance the dollar's normal-time financing and hedging benefits against sanctions-related disruptions to usable credit. The model identifies conditions under which greater working-capital dependence lowers the threshold for switching to RMB invoicing. In the reference quantitative specification, removing working-capital heterogeneity prevents the model from reproducing the low-WCI attenuation, even after re-fitting the remaining parameters. A separate retrospective comparison finds modest improvements in subsequent invoicing paths when working-capital heterogeneity is included. These findings point to the reliability of working-capital finance as a channel through which sanctions can reshape currency choice along trade links to China.
:::

</details>
